title: JavaScript & Engine Mastery
description: Scope, coercion, async execution, closures, event loop ordering, and prototype chains.

questions.question: What does 'typeof null' evaluate to in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: This is a historic JS bug. In original JS implementations, values were represented with type tags, and object's tag was 0. Since null was representation pointer NULL (0x00), typeof null evaluates to 'object'.

questions.question: Which of the following statements create block-scoped declarations in JavaScript? (Select all that apply)
options: function foo() {} in strict mode block
questions.explanation: let and const are block-scoped. Function declarations inside block statements are also block-scoped in ES6 strict mode. var is function-scoped or globally scoped.

questions.question: Order the steps of the JavaScript Event Loop execution order when a microtask and macrotask are scheduled:
items: Perform DOM Rendering / Repaint if necessary
correctOrder: Perform DOM Rendering / Repaint if necessary
questions.explanation: The Event Loop executes synchronous stack frames first, then flushes ALL pending microtasks, updates the UI/DOM render if needed, and finally pops ONE macrotask from the task queue.

questions.question: Match the JavaScript features to their respective concepts:

pairs.right: Rejects immediately if any input promise rejects
Waits for all promises to settle regardless of outcome
Settles with the result of the first promise that resolves or rejects
Fulfills with the first fulfilled promise, ignores rejections unless all fail

questions.explanation: Promise combinators have distinct settlement behaviors: all rejects fast, allSettled never rejects overall, race resolves/rejects with first result, and any looks for first success.

questions.question: What will be printed to the console when the following code executes?
questions.explanation: Synchronous logs run first ('A', 'D'). Then microtask Promise.then runs ('C'). Finally, macrotask setTimeout runs ('B'). Output: A, D, C, B.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the correct ES6 array method to check if at least one element passes a test function:
questions.explanation: Array.prototype.some() returns true if at least one array element passes the test implemented by the callback function.

title: React 19 & Hooks Deep Dive
description: Effects, transitions, stale closures, layout timing, and custom hook patterns.

questions.question: When should you use useLayoutEffect instead of useEffect?
options: When performing asynchronous data fetching calls
When you need to measure or write layout before browser paint to prevent visual flicker
Always, as it is faster than useEffect
questions.explanation: useLayoutEffect fires synchronously after all DOM mutations but before browser paint, preventing visual layout jumps during measurement.

questions.question: Which of the following are valid React 19 / Modern React rules or optimizations? (Select all that apply)
options: Hooks must only be called at the top level of function components
useActionState helps manage pending state for async form submissions
useEffect dependency arrays can safely contain unmemoized object literals created in render
useOptimistic enables optimistic UI updates during background server actions
questions.explanation: Hooks must follow top-level calling rules. React 19 introduced useActionState and useOptimistic. Unmemoized objects in useEffect dependency arrays cause infinite re-renders.

questions.question: Order the sequence of execution when a React state update occurs in a component with useEffect:
items: State update function (e.g. setState) is called
React renders component and generates new Virtual DOM
Browser paints updated DOM to screen
useEffect cleanup function runs for previous render
correctOrder: State update function (e.g. setState) is called
React renders component and generates new Virtual DOM
Browser paints updated DOM to screen
useEffect cleanup function runs for previous render
questions.explanation: React batches updates, renders Virtual DOM, applies mutations, allows browser paint, and asynchronously flushes passive effects (cleanups then callbacks).

questions.question: What issue exists in the following React component?
options: Infinite loop re-renders because count is in dependencies
Memory leak because setInterval is never cleared
Syntax error in cleanup function return
Stale closure bug: count inside setInterval is locked at 0, so count never increments beyond 1
questions.explanation: Because the dependency array is empty [], the closure captures count=0. Calling setCount(0+1) repeatedly sets count to 1. Fix by using functional update setCount(prev => prev + 1).

questions.question: Complete the Hook call to defer a non-urgent UI state recalculation during fast input typing:
questions.explanation: useDeferredValue accepts a value and returns a deferred copy that lags behind urgent state updates to keep rendering responsive.

title: Semantic HTML & CSS Layout
description: Semantic structure, the box model, specificity, and Flexbox layout fundamentals.

questions.question: Why is <section> generally preferred over <div> for a thematic grouping of content?
options: <section> is a semantic landmark that communicates meaning to assistive technology; <div> carries none
questions.explanation: Semantic elements like <section> give assistive technology and other tools real structural meaning that a generic <div> doesn't provide.

questions.question: Which of these increase a CSS selector's specificity? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: IDs, classes, and attribute selectors all add specificity. The universal selector (*) adds none.

questions.question: Order these from LOWEST to HIGHEST CSS specificity:
questions.explanation: Specificity increases from element < class < id < inline style, with !important overriding all of them regardless of specificity.

questions.question: Given `.card { padding: 16px; box-sizing: border-box; width: 200px; }`, what is the rendered content-box width?
questions.explanation: border-box makes padding and border count inward from the specified width, so the element stays 200px total while the content area shrinks to accommodate the 16px padding on each side.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the Flexbox property that distributes extra space between flex items (not around them):
questions.explanation: justify-content: space-between distributes extra space evenly between items, with no space before the first or after the last.

title: TypeScript Fundamentals
description: Type inference, unions and narrowing, generics, and typing real API data.

questions.question: What's the key difference between `any` and `unknown`?
options: unknown forces a narrowing check before use; any disables checking entirely
questions.explanation: unknown is the type-safe alternative to any -- it still accepts any value, but requires narrowing before you can operate on it.

questions.question: Which of these correctly narrow a `string | number` union inside an if block? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: typeof checks correctly narrow a string | number union. instanceof String and Array.isArray don't apply to this particular union.

questions.question: What does this generic function's return type resolve to when called as shown?
questions.explanation: TypeScript infers T as string from the array argument, so the generic function's return type resolves concretely to string for this call.

questions.question: Fill in the blank to model a field the API always sends but sometimes as null:
questions.explanation: A union with null (string | null) models a field that's always present but whose value can be null, distinct from an optional field with `?`.

questions.question: What does `res.json() as ApiUser` actually guarantee?
options: Nothing at runtime -- it's purely a compile-time promise to the type checker
A real runtime check that the response matches ApiUser
Automatic validation with a thrown error on mismatch
That the response is valid JSON
questions.explanation: Type assertions perform no runtime validation; if the real API response doesn't match, nothing catches the mismatch until something downstream breaks.

title: Testing with Vitest & React Testing Library
description: Unit vs. component vs. integration tests, RTL query priority, and avoiding over-mocking.

questions.question: What does an integration test verify that a unit test alone cannot?
options: That several real units actually work correctly together, not just in isolation
questions.explanation: Integration tests exercise multiple real pieces together, catching wiring problems that isolated unit tests can't surface.

questions.question: Which of these are reasons React Testing Library favors getByRole over getByTestId? (Select all that apply)
options: It mirrors how assistive technology perceives the page
It's the only query type available in RTL
A passing test doubles as a lightweight accessibility check
questions.explanation: Role-based queries reflect real user/assistive-tech perception of the page and act as a bonus accessibility signal -- getByTestId still exists and isn't deprecated, it's just a weaker signal.

questions.question: Order these steps of the arrange-act-assert testing pattern:
items: Render the component with initial props
Assert on the resulting visible output
correctOrder: Render the component with initial props
Assert on the resulting visible output
questions.explanation: Arrange (render with initial state) comes first, then act (simulate interaction), then assert (check the outcome).

questions.question: Why does this test fail to actually verify the intended behavior?
options: It mocks the exact validation logic it claims to test, and never asserts on the outcome
It uses the wrong button role
questions.explanation: The mock always returns true, so the real validation logic never runs -- and there's no assertion checking for the expected error message either.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the Testing Library API that mocks network requests at the network boundary:
questions.explanation: Mock Service Worker (MSW) intercepts requests at the network level, letting your real fetching code run against a faked server response.

title: Web Accessibility (WCAG) Fundamentals
description: Semantic interfaces, keyboard navigation, focus management, and accessible names.

questions.question: What is the 'first rule of ARIA'?
options: Add role attributes to every element
ARIA should only be used in forms
Use a native HTML element with the right semantics instead of patching a div with ARIA
questions.explanation: The first rule of ARIA use is to prefer a native element that already has the needed semantics and behavior, since ARIA alone doesn't grant things like keyboard interaction.

questions.question: Which of these are legitimate uses of tabindex="-1"? (Select all that apply)
options: Removing an element from the natural Tab sequence while still allowing programmatic focus
Moving focus into a modal on open via .focus()
Making an element the very first stop in Tab order
questions.explanation: tabindex="-1" removes an element from the Tab sequence but still allows it to receive focus programmatically -- exactly what's needed to move focus into a modal on open.

questions.question: What's wrong with this button in terms of accessibility?
options: It has no accessible name -- a screen reader announces it as just 'button' with no purpose
SVG can't be used inside a button
questions.explanation: An icon-only button with no text content or aria-label has no accessible name, so a screen reader user has no idea what it does.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the attribute that gives this icon-only button an accessible name:
questions.explanation: aria-label supplies an accessible name directly as a string, which is exactly what an icon-only button with no visible text needs.

questions.question: Why is `button:focus { outline: none; }` alone considered an accessibility regression?
options: It removes the only visual indicator of keyboard focus without providing any replacement
questions.explanation: Removing the focus outline with no replacement leaves keyboard users with no way to see where they currently are on the page.

title: Frontend Security: XSS, CSRF & CORS
description: Cross-site scripting, cross-site request forgery, CORS, and safe token storage.

questions.question:
Why is plain JSX interpolation like `

{text}

` safe from XSS by default?
options: JSX escapes interpolated values automatically instead of rendering them as executable HTML
questions.explanation: React's JSX interpolation escapes values by default -- the safety only breaks when you explicitly opt out with dangerouslySetInnerHTML or a similar API.

questions.question: Which of these mitigate CSRF? (Select all that apply)
options: Storing the token in localStorage instead of a cookie
questions.explanation: SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens directly address CSRF. The same-origin policy alone doesn't prevent it (it blocks reading the response, not sending the forged request), and moving to localStorage trades one risk (CSRF) for another (XSS-based token theft).

questions.question: What class of vulnerability does this code introduce if `text` comes from user input?
questions.explanation: Rendering untrusted content as raw HTML allows an attacker's injected script to execute in any other user's browser who views that content -- a classic stored XSS vector.

questions.question: Order these from LEAST to MOST protected token storage approach:
questions.explanation: localStorage and sessionStorage are both readable by any page JavaScript (XSS-vulnerable); httpOnly closes that gap but still needs Secure and SameSite to be fully protected against interception and CSRF.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the cookie flag that makes it invisible to JavaScript entirely:
questions.explanation: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie via document.cookie, closing the exact access an XSS payload would need to steal it.

title: Rendering Performance & Core Web Vitals
description: Memoization, code splitting, error boundaries, and measuring real performance.

questions.question: What does CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measure?
options: How much visible content unexpectedly shifts position during load
How long the largest element takes to render
How responsive the page is to clicks
questions.explanation: CLS captures unexpected visual movement during load -- content jumping just as a user is about to interact with it.

questions.question: Which of these directly reduce the amount of JavaScript shipped to the browser? (Select all that apply)
options: Using React Server Components for non-interactive content
questions.explanation: Code splitting, Server Components, and removing unused dependencies all reduce client bundle size. Adding more effects doesn't reduce bundle size.

questions.question: What's wrong with this error boundary usage?
options: ErrorBoundary must be a function component
A single app-wide boundary means any failure anywhere, even in StockTicker, blanks the entire page including Nav
questions.explanation: Wrapping the whole app in one boundary means a crash in any single risky component takes the entire page down -- boundaries should be scoped around specific risky sections.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the React API used to stream in a slow, non-critical section without blocking the rest of the page:
questions.explanation: Suspense lets a slow section render its fallback immediately while the rest of the page loads, streaming in the real content when ready.

questions.question: Why is Lighthouse data called 'lab data' rather than 'field data'?
options: It only works in a physical lab
It's a synthetic, single-run audit under simulated conditions, not a record of real user experience
questions.explanation: Lighthouse runs a controlled, simulated audit -- useful for catching regressions, but real field data from actual users reflects true device and network diversity.

title: Next.js Server Components & Rendering Strategy
description: Server vs. Client Components, data fetching, Server Actions, and choosing a rendering strategy.

questions.question: Why can't you use useState inside a Server Component?
options: Server Components render once on the server with no browser runtime for a hook to attach to
questions.explanation: Hooks like useState depend on a live browser runtime that re-renders on state changes -- Server Components produce static output on the server with no such runtime.

questions.question: Which of these require a Server Component to fetch data (rather than useEffect + fetch)? (Select all that apply)
options: A page's initial data that's known before the component mounts
Search-as-you-type results triggered by ongoing user interaction
A product page's description fetched from a database
Live-polling data that updates after the page has loaded
questions.explanation: Server Components handle a page's initial data well since they run before anything reaches the browser. Data that changes after load based on ongoing interaction (search-as-you-type, polling) still needs client-side fetching.

questions.question: What's the fix for this component, which only needs 'use client' for one small piece?
options: Remove 'use client' from ProductPage and extract LikeButton into its own small Client Component
Remove 'use client' from the whole file entirely
questions.explanation: Marking a whole page 'use client' to support one interactive piece loses server-rendering benefits for everything else; extracting just LikeButton keeps ProductPage as a Server Component.

questions.question: Order these rendering strategies from FRESHEST-per-request to LEAST fresh:
questions.explanation: SSR is freshest since it renders on every request; ISR refreshes periodically in the background; SSG is only as fresh as the last build with no further regeneration.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the directive that marks a function as callable directly from a form without a manually written API endpoint:
questions.explanation: 'use server' marks a function as a Server Action, letting Next.js handle the network call automatically when it's invoked from a form or client interaction.

title: Git & Version Control Workflow
description: Merge vs. rebase, resolving conflicts, and a professional PR workflow.

questions.question: What's the key difference between git merge and git rebase?
options: merge creates a new commit joining two histories; rebase replays commits on top of another branch for a linear history
rebase is only for deleting branches
merge only works on the main branch
questions.explanation: merge preserves both branches' history with a merge commit; rebase rewrites history to appear linear by replaying commits.

questions.question: What causes a merge conflict? (Select all that apply)
options: Both branches modified the same lines differently
One branch deleted a file the other branch modified
Both branches added the exact same new file with identical content
Git can't automatically determine how to reconcile the changes
questions.explanation: Conflicts arise when Git can't automatically reconcile changes -- typically overlapping edits or a delete/modify conflict. Identical additions merge cleanly without conflict.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the command that stages all changes in the current directory:
questions.explanation: git add . stages all changed files in the current directory (and below) for the next commit.

questions.question: What will happen when you run this sequence?
questions.codeSnippet:
git checkout feature-branch
git merge main
# main has a commit changing line 10 of app.js
# feature-branch has a different commit also changing line 10 of app.js
options: Git automatically creates a new file app.js.bak
Git reports a merge conflict on app.js and pauses for manual resolution
The merge is rejected entirely and no changes apply
questions.explanation: When both branches modify the same lines differently, Git can't automatically reconcile them and pauses with a merge conflict for manual resolution.

questions.question: What does `git rebase -i` (interactive rebase) commonly get used for?
options: Squashing, reordering, or editing commits before they're shared
questions.explanation: Interactive rebase lets you rewrite local commit history -- squashing related commits together, reordering them, or editing messages -- typically before pushing or opening a PR.

title: APIs, HTTP & Data Fetching
description: HTTP status codes, REST conventions, caching, and client-side data-fetching patterns.

questions.question: What's the difference between a 401 and a 403 HTTP status code?
options: 401 means authentication is missing/invalid; 403 means you're authenticated but not permitted
questions.explanation: 401 Unauthorized signals missing or invalid authentication; 403 Forbidden means you're authenticated but still not allowed to access the resource.

questions.question: Which of these HTTP methods are conventionally idempotent? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: GET, PUT, and DELETE are conventionally idempotent -- repeating them produces the same end state. POST typically is not, since repeating it can create duplicate resources.

questions.question: What does fetch() do when the server responds with a 500 status code?
options: fetch() throws, so this line never runs
res.ok is false, but the promise still resolves normally -- no automatic throw
res.ok is true because the request completed
The response body is automatically null
questions.explanation: fetch only rejects on genuine network failures, not on HTTP error statuses -- a 500 still resolves the promise, just with res.ok set to false, and you have to check it explicitly.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the HTTP method that applies a partial update to specific fields of a resource:
questions.template: fetch('/api/users/1', { method: '______', body: JSON.stringify({ name: 'New Name' }) });
questions.explanation: PATCH applies a partial update to specific fields; PUT is conventionally used to replace the entire resource.

questions.question: Order these caching freshness strategies from FRESHEST to LEAST fresh, per request:
questions.explanation: no-store always fetches fresh data; a revalidate interval refreshes periodically in the background; force-cache serves the same cached response indefinitely until invalidated.

title: Debugging & Reading Stack Traces
description: Reading stack traces, source maps, and systematic debugging under pressure.

questions.question: Why is a minified production stack trace hard to read without source maps?
options: Stack traces are disabled in production builds
Minified code strips readable names and collapses structure, so line/column numbers don't map to meaningful source locations
Source maps are only needed in development
questions.explanation: Minification trades readability for smaller bundle size; a source map is what lets an error tracker reconstruct the original file/line/function from a minified trace.

questions.question: Which of these are useful first steps when debugging an unfamiliar stack trace? (Select all that apply)
options: Identify which frame is actually in your own code vs. a library
Immediately rewrite the whole function from scratch
Check what the error message and error type actually say, not just the location
Reproduce it locally with the same inputs if possible
questions.explanation: Isolating your own code in the trace, reading the actual error message/type carefully, and reproducing locally are all productive first steps. Rewriting blind, before understanding the cause, tends to waste time or introduce new bugs.

questions.question: This error message is common in React apps. What's the most likely cause?
questions.codeSnippet: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
options: The component is missing a key prop
Code is calling .map() on a value that's undefined, often data that hasn't loaded yet
questions.explanation: This is a classic sign of calling .map() on data before it's actually loaded -- commonly needs a loading-state guard or a default empty array before the data arrives.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: an error boundary catches errors thrown during ______, but not inside event handlers.
questions.template: An error boundary catches errors thrown during ______, but not inside event handlers.
questions.explanation: Error boundaries catch errors in rendering, lifecycle methods, and constructors of their child tree -- event handler errors need their own try/catch.

questions.question: Why is 'thinking out loud' during a live debugging interview considered a good practice, not just filler talk?
options: It gives the interviewer visibility into your reasoning process, not just the eventual answer
It fills silence for its own sake
It's required by most interview platforms
It makes the debugging session shorter
questions.explanation: Narrating your reasoning lets an interviewer follow and evaluate your problem-solving process, which is often what's actually being assessed -- not just whether you land on the right answer.
